description:
We are a multidisciplinary team of five students from Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology (HCMUT) and Ho Chi Minh City University of Science (HCMUS), passionate about space exploration, aerospace engineering, and technology.
Our team combines knowledge of orbital mechanics, rocket propulsion, structural engineering, and engineering problem-solving with software development and programming experience.
summary:
An interactive, educational 3D space game that lets players experience the complete mission planning lifecycle from specification and design to inspection, launch, and orbital operations. Playing as a Chief Engineer under a greedy, penny-pinching Boss, you must build Earth-observation satellites for wildfire warning, space-weather defense, and climate monitoring on a severely limited budget. 
To address the challenges of making complex aerospace engineering accessible, the game combines an easy-to-follow tutorial, an engaging storyline, and real orbital physics and hardware specifications from NASA resources—teaching players how engineering trade-offs, thorough inspection, and refusing to cut corners directly impact both mission survival and life on Earth.
details:
How It Works:
"PHYSICS DOESN'T NEGOTIATE" runs as a 6-phase mission lifecycle across three escalating campaign levels—Wildfire Early Warning, Geomagnetic Storm Defense, and Methane Leak Monitoring. In Build Mode, players follow a 9-step sequential assembly flow (Orbit → Launch Vehicle → Bus → Instrument → Power → Battery → Comm → OBC → ADCS) supported by a real-time RK4 multi-stage trajectory preview and a minimalist 4-KPI dashboard (Power, Mass, Signal, Integrity). Following a "Launch Anything" philosophy, the system never blocks flawed designs; instead, players enter a timed 3D Pre-Flight Inspection darkroom to hunt down hidden physical defects using three specialized tools—an audio gas-leak detector, an X-ray crack scanner, and a camera tilt-alignment rig—before watching a full 3D Rocket Launch and a 12-Month Orbital Simulation. When budget cuts or tight deadlines from the Boss cause a satellite to fail in orbit, players receive a technical root-cause dossier and use evidence cards in a Boss Confrontation phase to win back funding and authority.

Tools, Languages & Architecture:
We built the project on a decoupled client–server architecture:

  • Backend: Python (3.11+), FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic v2, NumPy (for multi-stage RK4 orbital mechanics, physics kernels, and procedural 3D mesh generation), PyYAML (for mission packs, launch vehicles, and hardware catalogs), SQLite (session and replay persistence), and Pytest.
  • Frontend: React 18, Vite 6, JavaScript (ES Modules), CSS3 (industrial workshop aesthetic), and Three.js (0.172) for real-time 3D hangar assembly, X-ray inspection lighting, rocket launch FX, and orbital Earth visualization.

Creativity, Benefits & Intended Impact:
Rather than presenting aerospace engineering as dry spreadsheets, the project creatively merges satirical office drama (Papers, Please-style budget conflicts) with authentic physics (Apollo 13 / Kerbal-style failure analysis) and multi-sensory 3D inspection. Every technical outcome is tied directly to a Humanity Impact report—showing how a single under-specced antenna, unshielded computer, or missed assembly defect translates into lost forests, blacked-out power grids, or unchecked climate emissions. By letting players learn through safe, visual failure, the project aims to make STEM and space systems engineering accessible to students and enthusiasts while reinforcing engineering ethics under commercial pressure.

Key Factors Considered:
Our team carefully balanced physical realism vs. accessibility by keeping full orbital, power, eclipse, radiation, and downlink calculations in the backend while distilling player feedback into four clear KPIs and a step-by-step guided tutorial. We also prioritized data provenance transparency (documenting native, derived, and estimated hardware parameters) and browser 3D performance by generating procedural rocket and satellite meshes in NumPy and streaming compact buffers directly to Three.js.
